On 2/2011 she received the replacement mattress in which was made of foam (warranty exchange) the first night it was delivered she began to experience various different symptoms such as a burning eyes, rapid heart beat, difficult breathing.  There was a strong chemical odor off gassing from the mattress. She stopped sleeping on the mattress and began to sleep on her couch and closed the door to the bedroom to eliminate the odor. 
The symptoms began to get worse she had a sore throat upper respiratory infection and went to the doctor where she was diagnosed with having asthma. The doctor also stated that she developed a chemical sensitivity and has the lungs of an 83 year old woman, she got the second mid late February and this was all coil. The mattress both had the same retardant but this mattress is less of it. She contacted the retailer in which they came out to the home to exchange the mattress with a new one.

On 2/15/2011 she had possession of the new  mattress in which was made with coils for one day and when she walked in the room her eyes immediately began to itch and burn. The mattress was left in the hallway of her home. She then pushed it into the bedroom and closed the door to the room and continued to sleep on her couch.


She contacted the retailer and they are willing to allow her to return the mattress to exchange it with a new one. The second mattress did not have as much of a toxic smell coming from the mattes as the first one did. She contacted the firm and they are interested in sending out an investigator to take a look at the mattress.

incident_description: A new style of compact fluorescent lamp is very prone to breakage, releasing Mercury into the air and creating a broken glass hazzard.  I purchased a ceiling mounted light fixture at Lowes.  It came with a Good Earth Lighting 27W CFL Model B2427-30-SP also labelled "E300850 Lamp Adapter 61Y6".  This lamp resembles in every way the standard CFL "screw base" but instead it has two pins.  It appears to be a standard screw base lamp with an "adapter" to the two-pin socket.  However, applying light twisting pressure to the lamp causes the glass envelope to break, releasing Mercury and gas into the air and causing a broken glass hazzard.  This style of lamp should be clearly labelled as NOT being a screw-in base, and should NOT be labelled as an "adapter", which implies it adapts standard screw-in lamps to the two-pin socket.
justification: The incident describes a hazardous situation with potential for injury due to broken glass and mercury release, but no actual injury is reported.

I could see the wires were exposed in two places on the cord (they'd burst out) and there was smoke coming from the holder itself. I had to get the thing unplugged and bring it out of the house.

The bulbs are completely exposed, not enclosed or covered in the fixture in anyway.  After the light was on for a few minutes, the bulb got extremely hot and starting smoking, would very likely have caused a fire if we were not present in the room when this occured.  I dissembled the fixture to see if there was anything amiss with it. Fixture itself is completely fine, and we experienced no problem with the replacement bulb. incident_description:
My wife and I purchased a leather sofa from Bob's Discount Furniture in Yonkers, New York in March 2011.  From the day it arrived we noticed a chemical odor.  For the next several weeks we noticed that every time we would sit on the soda for long periods of time we would have an apparent allergic reaction.  For my wife it was a severe headache, itchy skin, coughing and sneezing.  For me it was similar to an asmatic reaction accompanied by an abnormal heart rhythm.

Today I read an article on the Internet from the Sydney Herald (Australia) published on April 13, 2009 which reported that:

 "A toxic fungicide, Dimethyl fumarate, in the form of a fine, white crystalline powder, was found in sachets embedded in the furniture sourced to China. It is believed the body heat generated from sitting on a contaminated couch causes a toxic vapour to seep out."

[redacted] from Melbourne's Skin and Cancer Foundation, said although there have been no reported cases in Australia, people may not have made a link between a skin outbreak and their couch.

"The rashes can be quite severe, this chemical is a really strong allergen," she said.

"It can make the skin itchy enough to prevent sleep, and cortisone creams and sometimes even cortisone tablets are needed to calm it down."

About 200,000 of the suspect couches have been imported by 15 furniture retailers in Britain alone and compensation for victims, some of whom required hospital treatment, could be in the tens of millions of dollars.

The European Union and British governments ordered a recall of all products containing dimethyl fumarate late last month."

Consumer Reports also reported on this matter in 2009.

We wish to know if there is any kind of governmental action taking place agianst either the Chinese manufacturers and or the U.S. retailers selling these toxic sofas.  We also wish to know how many, if any, U.S. Citizens have reported a similar complaint.
justification: The incident caused allergic reactions and health issues (injury), but the likelihood is unlikely as it's a specific chemical issue from a particular source.

My son is aprox 9lb, so exactly in the size range and still has several inches growth room at the bottom.  However, from the first use he's been able to get his hands out the neck hole.  I wasn't as concerned about this and thought maybe it was good - he likes his hand by his face so he could self soothe and still be in the swaddle.  After 2 uses he was able to get his whole arm out. which is more concerning to me safety wise and this morning I woke to find him with the fabric up over his face, struggling to get it off.  If the fabric can cover his face it seems this could be a SIDS risk - no matter how thin the fabric!  After all, parents are admonished not to use any loose blankets - even thin ones - in a crib due to suffocation and smothering concerns.  A brief google search to determine if I had a defective item revealed this as a common complaint (Neck hole too large allowing arms out and fabric covering faces).  I love the concept of the product  - mimics the womb, allows movement but not TOO freely - and my son sleeps great in it, but I think it needs a design tweak to make the neck hole smaller to prevent this from occurring.  I'll also be CCing this to the CPSC for review.

Unfortunately, since I have used and washed the product, Babies R Us won't take it back, so my money is wasted since I will no longer use the product.  I hope your company will look into this and correct it before a child is injured!

Sincerely,

[REDACTED]

We have purchased four of these ceiling fixtures for our home, two in our kitchen and two in our hallway. We purchased them at different times, but all within the last two years.

About 3 months ago I was cooking in the kitchen when suddenly the glass shade from the ceiling lamp crashed to the floor and broke into hundreds of pieces. It was very shocking as I had been standing directly under the lamp just seconds before it fell. We could not understand why this happened as it had been properly installed and certainly seemed secure. However, since no one was hurt, we shrugged our shoulders and bought another lamp.

Just two weeks ago, however, the very same thing happened with one of the lamps in our downstairs hallway. We were all upstairs when there was a huge crash and, once again, the ceiling fixture glass shade was on the floor in many pieces! Certainly this could not be a coincidence, so we looked very carefully at the way the lamp was secured to the ceiling. 

What my husband discovered was this: the nipple (Part F in Portfolio Package Contents diagram) came out of the coupling (Part D). In fact, the coupling seemed very loose ÃÂ as if it might have expanded with heat. My husband is certain that this was not the case when we installed the lamp.

If two of these ceiling lamps fell in our home, we feel there is a good chance it could happen to other customers. It does appear that the coupling is made of very poor material ÃÂ it is manufactured in China ÃÂ and does not securely hold the lamp to the ceiling for an extended period of time. This is a situation which if not investigated now could prove harmful ÃÂ or deadly ÃÂ to others in the future.

Thank you for your time in this matter.
justification: The incident describes two occurrences of ceiling lamp failures causing glass shades to fall, with no injuries reported but potential for harm.

incident_description:

incident_description:

In order to hang the pictures, a decorative piece (looks like a truck wheel) is attached to the wall with a picture hanger. The actual picture itself has a piece of ribbon on each of the top corners and the ribbons are supposed to be tied to the wheel on the wall. incident_description:

incident_description:
I am contacting you in the hopes that you will take action to help prevent other consumers from making a significant investment in furniture that literally falls apart and presents a safety hazard to families with young children.   

In its corporate marketing materials, La-Z-boy promises furniture made with "durability,ÃÂ "high standards,ÃÂ "wear tested fabrics,ÃÂ and "superior qualityÃÂ ÃÂ however my actual experience with the furniture has been dramatically to the contrary ÃÂ and the company refuses to properly address potentially dangerous quality issues.

I purchased a leather couch and loveseat from La-Z-boy approximately five years ago.  I invested $3000 in the set ÃÂ and was assured that these leather pieces would be able to stand the test of time. After only 2.5 years, the leather began pulling away on the arm of the couch, exposing sharp staples.  I contacted the company and communicated that I was concerned about the quality of the piece and its potential longevity.  After extensive follow up, they finally agreed to send an upholsterer to repair the piece. 

A few years later, in the Fall of 2010, we again faced another significant quality issue - the plastic piping began popping through the loveseat cushions, creating an area with exposed plastic piping that is approximately 10-12 inches long presenting a choking hazard for our 2-year old. We again contacted the company ÃÂ and they have refused to do anything about the furniture, but rather focused on shifting blame indicating that we must have caused the damage -- even though for the vast majority of the life of the furniture, it was only being used by two adults and we also purchased the leather protection treatment when we first invested in the piece. 

Since our rejected La-Z-boy inquiry, we contacted a Boston area leather repair company to assess the furniture for repair.  The representative of this company visited our home in January and estimated that it would likely be too costly to justify repairing the piece. This representative also indicated that the most likely cause of the piping issue was not in fact user wear, but rather poor manufacturing using leather that was too thin to encase the piping to fully protect it from breaking through the leather.

For your reference, I am attaching photos of the La-Z-boy furniture.  I truly hope you will be able to make this company accountable for the quality issues we have experienced.  I also strongly encourage you to investigate how many other pieces from the same manufacturing batch could be affected with either exposed staples and/or piping to prevent any other families from a potentially dangerous situation that could harm their young children. 

If you have any questions, feel free to contact me. Also, I would love to be kept abreast of your investigation if possible. 

Best regards, 
***
justification: The incident describes furniture defects (exposed staples and piping) that present a safety hazard, but no actual injury is reported.

incident_description:
The product is a drop leaf table, produced by Ashley Furniture, Model number D319-23.  The leafs are supposed to be held on by hinges with pins running through them.  These pins have come loose in the past and we have put them back in.  Today when my 4 year old daughter was coloring at the table, the drop leaf (which was up in table position) came completely loose, swung up (pivoting on the arm that holds the weight of the leaf), hit her in the head knocking her into another corner on the table and off her seat onto the floor.  She has severe bruising as a result.  
When we put the leaf back on the table, we noticed that 6 of the original 12 pins that hold both leafs on the table are missing.  We never noticed these pins fall out, and do not know where they are.  
We use this table in a normal manner, and have not done anything that would cause these pins to fall out.  We rarely fold the leaves in and out.  We only use the table for dining, homework, and child artwork.  We do not place excessive weight on the table.  These pins are just falling out on their own, without us doing anything to cause the pins to fall out of the hinges.  Without secure pins, the table leafs are prone to coming loose and falling apart.  The manufacturer defect is in the design of the hinges and pins, in which the pins are coming loose on their own when they should not.  The table is approximately 2 years old.  

We consider ourselves lucky, these injuries could have been much worse.  She could have landed in a worse position.  What if there was a fresh cup of hot coffee on the table leaf that broke?  What if she was cutting with her scissors? The potential for injury with the poor hinge and pin design is much more serious than what we experienced.  Obviously, a table that just falls apart during normal usage is hazardous.
justification: The incident resulted in severe bruising to a child, indicating an injury (severity level 3). The pins have repeatedly come loose without cause, suggesting a high likelihood of recurrence (occurrence likelihood 4).

incident_description:

- On Mar 10 2011 the second light bulb suddenly exploded the very first time I tried using it (after changing the prior bulb), the moment I turned on the light switch. incident_description: Tempur-Pedic mattress stole my health and my home.  I had a new Tempur-Pedic  Cloud Lux delivered exactly one week ago, and my health deteriorated from the very first night. Their customer service line gave me no help whatsoever.  They said this was between me and the store that I bought the mattress from.  I want my money, my home and my health back.

incident_description:
I am writing to describe a near miss fire in my home.

A GE helical 20W CFL light bulb hanging in basement almost caught fire.

From the bulb base:

HELICAL 20W
120 VAC, 60Hz, 300 mA
FLE20HT3/2/SW
made in China

I was in the basement doing work and smelled burning plastic, looking around for the source, it was apparent that the CFL was burning internally in the ballast portion of the bulb.

There were visible sparks inside the plastic ballast, smoke was coming out of the ballast portion, and the plastic encapsulating the ends the glass helix had melted, with the helix hanging at an odd angle.

I unscrewed the bulb using an insulating cloth, the unit was very hot to the touch.  I am certain it would have continued to burn if I had not cut the power off.
